title: Methods of prescribing relative exercise intensity: physiological and practical considerations
authors: Mann T, Lamberts RP, Lambert MI
population: Review of %VO2max, %HRmax, %VO2R, %HRR (Karvonen), aerobic-threshold and anaerobic-threshold intensity prescription
findings: Exercise at a fixed %VO2max or %HRmax does not necessarily place individuals at an equivalent intensity above resting levels; some are above and others below the aerobic or anaerobic threshold at the same percentage.
Fixed %VO2max/%HRmax produces interindividual variation in blood lactate, and a similar effect has been shown for %VO2R and %HRR.

Threshold-relative prescription is expected to give less individual variation in metabolic response and time to exhaustion, but many of these theoretical advantages have not been directly demonstrated.
Thresholds from a single incremental test cannot be assumed accurate without verification trials and tend to show higher day-to-day variation than VO2max or HRmax.
limitations: Narrative review; the claimed advantages of threshold-based prescription are described as largely not yet demonstrated; no numeric zone boundaries.
implications: Prefer threshold-anchored zones (LT1/VT1 and CS or LT2) when data exist; do not present %HRmax zones as physiologically equivalent between athletes.

Heart rate reserve (Karvonen) is not shown here to be better than %HRmax, since similar lactate variation was reported for %HRR; the review gives no basis to rank them, so HRR is an acceptable fallback only when resting HR is reliably known.
Because thresholds vary day to day, re-estimate them from rolling recent data and give them a tolerance band rather than a single fixed value.
No specific %HRR cut-offs are justified by this paper.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (vol 43 pp 613-625). Abstract confirms all statements. Researcher's implication that HRR is preferable to raw %HRmax was not supported (abstract says HRR also shows interindividual variation); rewritten.
